questions.q: Which mechanism best explains the abrupt pressure rise in acute angle-closure glaucoma?
ch: Increased outflow resistance at an anatomically open trabecular meshwork
Ciliary body shutdown with markedly reduced aqueous humor production
The peripheral iris bows forward and occludes the trabecular meshwork, halting aqueous drainage
Choroidal neovascular membranes leaking fluid beneath the central retina
Separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.exp: In angle closure the peripheral iris bows forward against the trabecular meshwork so aqueous cannot drain, and intraocular pressure rises abruptly, often above 40-50 mmHg, compressing the optic nerve.
why: That describes primary open-angle glaucoma, where the angle stays open and resistance rises within the meshwork.
Aqueous production is not shut off; treatment actually works by suppressing production pharmacologically.
Choroidal neovascularization is the wet macular degeneration mechanism, not an aqueous outflow problem.
Separation of the retina from the pigment epithelium is retinal detachment and does not raise pressure.

questions.q: On examination of a patient in an acute angle-closure attack, what is the expected pupil finding?
ch: A fixed mid-dilated 4-6 mm pupil that is non-reactive to light
A pinpoint pupil that constricts briskly to a light stimulus
A fully dilated pupil that still reacts normally to bright light
A small, irregular pupil of the kind described in anterior uveitis
A relative afferent pupillary defect with an otherwise normal pupil size
questions.exp: The module describes a fixed mid-dilated 4-6 mm non-reactive pupil as the sweet spot for pupillary block, together with a hazy steamy cornea and ciliary (perilimbal) injection.
why: The pupil in an attack is mid-dilated and poorly reactive rather than small and briskly reactive.
The pupil sits mid-dilated, not fully dilated, and it does not react normally to light.
A constricted pupil is characteristic of anterior uveitis, which the module contrasts with angle closure.
An afferent pupillary defect is described with large retinal detachments, not with angle closure.

questions.q: Which classic triad does the module give for acute angle-closure glaucoma?
ch: Bilateral itching, stringy mucoid discharge, and cobblestone papillae
Drusen, wavy distorted lines, and a dense central scotoma
Painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and halos around lights
Flashes, floaters, and a curtain descending over the visual field
Painless peripheral field loss, optic disc cupping, and an open angle
questions.exp: The classic triad is a painful red eye plus a fixed mid-dilated pupil plus halos around lights, often accompanied by headache, nausea, and vomiting.
why: Itching with stringy discharge and lid papillae describes allergic conjunctivitis.
Drusen with distortion and a central scotoma point to age-related macular degeneration.
Flashes, floaters, and an advancing curtain are the retinal detachment warning sequence.
Painless field loss with cupping and an open angle describes primary open-angle glaucoma.

questions.q: A patient with a shallow anterior chamber develops an acute attack shortly after taking an over-the-counter cold remedy. Which drug property precipitated it?
ch: Anticholinergic mydriatic effect that mid-dilates the pupil into the danger zone
Cholinergic agonism producing pupillary constriction
Prostaglandin-mediated increase in uveoscleral outflow
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reducing aqueous formation
Beta-blockade reducing aqueous humor production
questions.exp: Mydriatic and anticholinergic drugs — decongestants, antihistamines, TCAs, dilating drops — mid-dilate the pupil and precipitate pupillary block in a small, crowded, shallow-chambered eye.
why: Cholinergic agonists such as pilocarpine constrict the pupil and are used to reopen the angle.
Prostaglandin analogs increase outflow and lower pressure; they are open-angle therapy, not a trigger.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition lowers intraocular pressure and is part of treating the attack.
Beta-blocker drops lower pressure by reducing aqueous production and are first-line here.

questions.q: Why does the module warn that pilocarpine is often ineffective early in an acute attack?
ch: It is inactivated by the steamy edematous cornea and never reaches the anterior chamber
It works only after a laser peripheral iridotomy has already been performed
It requires an intact trabecular meshwork in order to increase aqueous outflow
It transiently raises intraocular pressure further before it starts to lower it
At very high pressure the iris sphincter is ischemic and paralyzed, so miotics fail until pressure drops
questions.exp: The pilocarpine paradox: markedly elevated pressure leaves the iris sphincter ischemic and unresponsive, so the drug must be given after the pressure-lowering agents and never relied on alone.
why: Corneal edema is listed as an examination finding, not as a mechanism that inactivates the drug.
Pilocarpine is given before laser iridotomy as a medical step to reopen the angle, not after it.
Pilocarpine works by pulling the iris off the meshwork mechanically, not by requiring its function.
No paradoxical pressure rise is described; the problem is an unresponsive, ischemic iris sphincter.

questions.q: Which nursing action does the module specify for a patient in an acute angle-closure attack?
ch: Apply firm pressure over the closed globe to help drive aqueous out
Position the patient supine so the lens falls back off the iris, and keep the room comfortably lit
Place the patient in high Fowler's position with the head of the bed fully upright
Darken the room completely to reduce photophobia and eye discomfort
Instill a mydriatic drop so the ophthalmologist can view the fundus
questions.exp: Lying supine lets the lens fall back off the iris, and a comfortably lit room avoids further pupil dilation; a dark room would widen the pupil and worsen the block.
why: No pressure maneuver on the globe is described; palpation is only a gentle bedside check.
Sitting fully upright is not the recommended position; the module directs supine positioning.
A dark room dilates the pupil further and is exactly what the module says to avoid.
Dilating drops are contraindicated — flag any mydriatic or anticholinergic order in this patient.

questions.q: A 68-year-old hyperopic woman has severe right eye pain, halos, vomiting, and a rock-hard globe with an intraocular pressure of 56 mmHg. Topical timolol, brimonidine, and dorzolamide have been given. What does the module describe next?
ch: Topical atropine to relax the ciliary body and deepen the anterior chamber
Urgent trabeculectomy with a glaucoma drainage implant to bypass the meshwork
Observation with serial tonometry every four hours until the pressure normalizes
Immediate laser peripheral iridotomy performed through the edematous, steamy cornea
Systemic acetazolamide and IV mannitol to crash the pressure, then pilocarpine to reopen the angle
questions.exp: The acute sequence is to crash the pressure with topical agents plus systemic acetazolamide and IV mannitol, and only then give pilocarpine to pull the iris off the meshwork; laser follows once the cornea clears.
why: Atropine is an anticholinergic mydriatic — exactly the class that precipitates an attack.
Trabeculectomy and drainage implants are open-angle surgical options for failed medical therapy.
Observation is unsafe; the module stresses that vision loss here is time-critical.
Laser peripheral iridotomy is definitive but waits until the cornea clears and the pressure falls.

questions.q: Before giving systemic acetazolamide during an acute attack, which history would the module have you flag?
ch: Prior uncomplicated cataract surgery in the affected eye
Sickle cell disease with a documented sulfa allergy and severe renal impairment
Well-controlled hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic
Hyperopia with a shallow anterior chamber in the fellow eye
A family history of primary open-angle glaucoma in two siblings
questions.exp: Acetazolamide is avoided in sulfa allergy, sickle cell disease, and severe renal impairment, and hypokalemia with metabolic acidosis must be monitored whenever it is used.
why: Prior cataract surgery is a retinal detachment risk factor and does not preclude acetazolamide.
Thiazide-treated hypertension is not a listed contraindication, though electrolytes still need monitoring.
A narrow fellow eye is expected here and is an indication for prophylactic iridotomy, not a drug bar.
Family history matters for open-angle glaucoma risk, not as an acetazolamide contraindication.

questions.q: What does the module identify as the definitive treatment, and what does it say about the fellow eye?
ch: Trabeculectomy in the affected eye only, with pressure-lowering drops for the fellow eye
Lifelong pilocarpine in both eyes, with no procedure required at any point
Selective laser trabeculoplasty in the affected eye and annual screening of the fellow eye
Laser peripheral iridotomy, with prophylactic iridotomy of the fellow eye because it shares the anatomy
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection, repeated in the fellow eye if the pressure rises
questions.exp: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates an alternate aqueous pathway and is definitive; the anatomically narrow fellow eye is treated prophylactically because it shares the same crowded anatomy.
why: Trabeculectomy is a surgical option in open-angle disease, not the definitive fix for pupillary block.
Pilocarpine is a temporizing medical step and cannot substitute for the definitive laser procedure.
Laser trabeculoplasty targets the trabecular meshwork in open-angle glaucoma, not a closed angle.
Anti-VEGF injections treat neovascular macular disease and have no definitive role in angle closure.

questions.q: A patient presents with headache, intractable nausea and vomiting, and blurred vision with halos. Why does the module insist you examine and palpate the eye?
ch: Because visual acuity is normal in angle closure and confirms a neurologic cause
Because vomiting itself raises the intraocular pressure and must first be quantified
Because the differential is limited to migraine and requires imaging before treatment
Because these symptoms can masquerade as migraine or a GI emergency while the eye is the source
Because antiemetics cannot be given until the corneal reflex has been documented
questions.exp: Halos with nausea and vomiting are easily mistaken for migraine or an acute abdomen; palpating a rock-hard globe and finding a fixed mid-dilated pupil identifies the ocular source.
why: Vision is blurred with halos in angle closure, so normal acuity would not be expected.
Vomiting is a symptom of the pressure spike, not the cause of it, in this module's account.
The differential is broader — anterior uveitis, keratitis, endophthalmitis, scleritis — and treatment must not wait for imaging.
No such requirement exists; antiemetics and a quiet environment are part of supportive care.

questions.q: Which description best characterizes primary open-angle glaucoma?
ch: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium
An acute, painful optic neuropathy with a closed angle and a rock-hard globe
A chronic, painless optic neuropathy with an anatomically open anterior chamber angle
A degenerative disease of the macula producing drusen and central vision loss
Inflammation of the conjunctiva with discharge and a normal visual acuity
questions.exp: Open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, painless, progressive optic neuropathy in which gonioscopy confirms that the angle between iris and cornea is open, distinguishing it from angle-closure.
why: Separation of the retina from the pigment epithelium is retinal detachment.
Acute pain with a closed angle and a hard globe describes acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Drusen with central loss describes age-related macular degeneration, not an optic neuropathy.
Conjunctival inflammation with discharge describes conjunctivitis, which spares the optic nerve.

questions.q: Why does the module call primary open-angle glaucoma the "silent thief of sight"?
ch: It causes sudden painless central vision loss with wavy, distorted straight lines
It produces halos and severe eye pain that patients often attribute to a migraine
It is asymptomatic because intraocular pressure stays within the normal range in every case
It is painless and takes peripheral vision first, sparing central acuity until late, so patients present dangerously late
It only begins to progress after an optic disc hemorrhage announces itself on fundoscopy
questions.exp: Peripheral vision is lost painlessly first while central acuity is spared until advanced disease, so patients notice nothing and present late — and vision already lost cannot be recovered.
why: Sudden central loss with metamorphopsia is the wet macular degeneration picture, not glaucoma.
Halos with severe pain belong to acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is anything but silent.
Only up to a third of cases occur at statistically normal pressures; elevated pressure is typical.
A disc hemorrhage is a red flag for ongoing progression, not the point at which damage begins.

questions.q: Which fundoscopic finding supports a diagnosis of primary open-angle glaucoma?
ch: Cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.5 with rim thinning or notching and a disc hemorrhage
Yellow drusen deposits and pigment changes clustered at the macula
An elevated, corrugated, mobile retina with a visible peripheral tear
A gray-green subretinal membrane with hemorrhage and hard exudate
Cobblestone papillae seen on the everted upper eyelid
questions.exp: The module lists a cup-to-disc ratio above 0.5, disc asymmetry, thinning or notching of the neuroretinal rim, and disc hemorrhages as the hallmark structural findings.
why: Macular drusen and pigment change are the findings of dry age-related macular degeneration.
An elevated, corrugated, mobile retina with a tear indicates rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
A gray-green subretinal membrane with hemorrhage describes choroidal neovascularization in wet AMD.
Cobblestone papillae on the lid are an allergic conjunctivitis finding, not an optic disc sign.

questions.q: Why does the module insist on interpreting intraocular pressure alongside central corneal thickness?
ch: Corneal thickness determines whether the anterior chamber angle is open or closed
Pachymetry replaces Goldmann applanation as the reference standard for pressure
Corneal thickness predicts how well the patient will respond to prostaglandin analogs
Thin corneas under-read pressure and are themselves an independent risk factor for progression
Thick corneas make gonioscopy impossible and must therefore be excluded first
questions.exp: Goldmann applanation readings must be interpreted against central corneal thickness from pachymetry, because thin corneas underestimate pressure and independently raise progression risk — a key OHTS lesson.
why: The angle is established by gonioscopy, not inferred from corneal thickness measurements.
Goldmann applanation remains the reference for pressure; pachymetry only helps interpret it.
No relationship between corneal thickness and prostaglandin response is described here.
Gonioscopy is performed to confirm an open angle regardless of how thick the cornea measures.

questions.q: A patient started on latanoprost asks what to expect. Which counseling point does the module give?
ch: Expect wheezing and a slow pulse from systemic absorption of the drop
Expect whorl-like corneal deposits and marked conjunctival hyperemia
Expect iris and periocular darkening plus increased eyelash growth
Expect fatigue and an allergic conjunctivitis reaction to the drop
Expect paresthesias, metabolic acidosis, and a low potassium level
questions.exp: Prostaglandin analogs are first-line for potency and once-daily dosing, but they cause iris and periocular darkening, eyelash growth, and orbital fat atrophy.
why: Wheezing and bradycardia come from systemically absorbed beta-blocker drops such as timolol.
Corneal verticillata with hyperemia are the rho kinase inhibitor (netarsudil) effects.
Fatigue and allergic conjunctivitis are described with the alpha-2 agonist brimonidine.
Paresthesias, acidosis, and hypokalemia are effects of oral acetazolamide.

questions.q: Which drop-instillation teaching does the module give to limit systemic absorption of timolol?
ch: Rest the bottle tip against the lashes to steady the hand during instillation
Instill two drops in rapid succession to guarantee that an adequate dose reaches the eye
Instill all of the prescribed drops back to back so that none of them is forgotten
Rinse the eye with sterile saline immediately after each drop has been instilled
One drop, then punctal occlusion and eyelid closure for about one minute, waiting five minutes between different drops
questions.exp: Punctal occlusion — pressing the inner corner — with the eyelid closed for roughly a minute reduces systemic absorption, and different drops are spaced about five minutes apart.
why: Touching the bottle tip to the lashes or eye is exactly what the module warns against.
A single drop is taught; a second drop adds systemic exposure without added benefit.
Different drops must be separated by about five minutes rather than given back to back.
Rinsing would wash the medication away; the module teaches eyelid closure instead.

questions.q: A patient has classic disc cupping and arcuate field defects but every pressure reading is under 21 mmHg. How does the module frame this?
ch: A normal examination, because glaucoma cannot occur at pressures below 21 mmHg
Normal-tension glaucoma — treat by lowering pressure anyway and consider vascular and secondary contributors
Ocular hypertension without glaucoma, so neither treatment nor further follow-up is needed
Acute angle-closure disease that has been intermittently decompressing itself over time
Age-related macular degeneration presenting unusually with a peripheral field defect
questions.exp: Up to a third of open-angle glaucoma occurs at statistically normal pressures; normal-tension glaucoma is still treated by lowering pressure, with vascular and secondary causes considered.
why: The module states explicitly that typical damage occurs at pressures under 21 mmHg.
There is documented disc and field damage, so this is glaucoma needing treatment, not mere ocular hypertension.
Angle closure is acute, painful, and red, and nothing here suggests a closed angle on gonioscopy.
Macular degeneration takes central vision and spares the periphery — the opposite pattern.

questions.q: Which option does the module offer specifically to sidestep problems with drop adherence?
ch: Oral acetazolamide once daily as a long-term substitute for all topical therapy
A trabeculectomy performed at the time of diagnosis in every patient
Switching from a prostaglandin analog to a topical beta-blocker instead
Prescribing an AREDS2 supplement to slow structural progression
Selective laser trabeculoplasty, usable first-line or as an adjunct and repeatable over time
questions.exp: Selective laser trabeculoplasty improves trabecular outflow, can be first-line or adjunctive, is repeatable, and avoids the adherence problems of drops — a patient-centered point worth volunteering.
why: Oral acetazolamide is reserved for short-term or large reductions and causes paresthesias and acidosis.
Trabeculectomy is reserved for progressive or advanced disease after medications and laser fail.
Swapping one drop for another does not address adherence and adds beta-blocker contraindications.
AREDS2 supplements are for intermediate or advanced macular degeneration, not for glaucoma.

questions.q: How does the module say a target pressure should be expressed?
ch: As a set percentage reduction from that patient's own baseline pressure
As the pressure at which the cup-to-disc ratio returns toward normal
As the pressure at which the visual field defects reverse and disappear
As a single universal number below 21 mmHg applied to every patient
As whatever value the patient's thinnest corneal reading happens to produce
questions.exp: Management is target-pressure driven: lower the pressure by a set percentage from baseline rather than aiming at one magic number, and let disease staging drive follow-up intervals.
why: Cupping does not reverse; the structural damage from lost ganglion cells is permanent.
Field defects do not reverse — vision that has already been lost cannot be recovered.
The module explicitly rejects a single magic number in favor of a percentage reduction.
Corneal thickness informs how a reading is interpreted, not what the target should be.

questions.q: A treated patient's pressure is at target, but a new splinter disc hemorrhage and a deepening arcuate scotoma appear. What does the module advise?
ch: Continue the current therapy unchanged, since the pressure target has already been met
Escalate therapy urgently — a disc hemorrhage with field progression signals active damage
Stop all of the drops and observe for six months before repeating the visual fields
Refer the patient for laser peripheral iridotomy of both eyes
Begin intravitreal anti-VEGF injections to protect the remaining optic nerve fibers
questions.exp: A new splinter disc hemorrhage or documented field and OCT progression means damage is ongoing, so therapy is escalated even when the numbers look acceptable.
why: The module warns against anchoring on an acceptable number when the disc or fields are worsening.
Stopping therapy allows silent progression, which is the opposite of what is advised.
Iridotomy relieves pupillary block in angle closure; this patient's angle is open.
Anti-VEGF therapy targets choroidal neovascularization in wet AMD, not glaucomatous neuropathy.

questions.q: The module names viral conjunctivitis as the most common form. Which organism is usually responsible?
ch: Chlamydia trachomatis
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Adenovirus
Staphylococcus aureus
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
questions.exp: Viral conjunctivitis is the most common form and is usually adenoviral — self-limited over one to two weeks and highly contagious, so hand hygiene is emphasized.
why: Chlamydia causes adult inclusion and neonatal conjunctivitis, not the most common form.
Pseudomonas is the organism feared in contact-lens-related corneal ulcer, not the usual cause.
S. aureus is a bacterial cause, but bacterial conjunctivitis is less common than viral disease.
Gonococcus causes hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis — an emergency, but an uncommon one.

questions.q: According to the module, which discharge pattern points to bacterial conjunctivitis?
ch: Stringy mucoid discharge with intense bilateral itching
Thick purulent discharge with eyelids stuck shut in the morning
No discharge at all, with photophobia and a ciliary flush
Clear tearing with normal lids and cobblestone papillae
Watery discharge with a tender preauricular lymph node
questions.exp: Thick purulent discharge — classically eyelids stuck shut on waking — points to a bacterial etiology, whereas a watery discharge suggests viral or allergic disease.
why: Stringy mucoid discharge with bilateral itching is the allergic pattern.
Photophobia with a ciliary flush is a red flag for keratitis, uveitis, or angle closure.
Cobblestone papillae with clear tearing are allergic findings, not bacterial ones.
Watery discharge with a tender preauricular node strongly suggests viral (adenoviral) disease.

questions.q: Which cluster of findings does the module give for allergic conjunctivitis?
ch: Unilateral hyperacute copious purulent discharge within 12 to 24 hours
Watery discharge with a tender preauricular lymph node and lid follicles
Reduced visual acuity with severe pain and a fluorescein-staining dendrite
Purulent discharge in a neonate on the third or fourth day of life
Bilateral intense itching, stringy mucoid discharge, cobblestone papillae, and rhinitis
questions.exp: Allergic disease is bilateral with intense itching, stringy mucoid discharge, cobblestone papillae, and associated rhinitis or atopy; it is IgE and mast-cell mediated.
why: Hyperacute copious purulent discharge over 12-24 hours is gonococcal until proven otherwise.
Watery discharge with a preauricular node and follicles indicates viral conjunctivitis.
Reduced acuity, pain, and a dendrite mean herpetic keratitis — an emergency, not allergy.
Neonatal purulent discharge is ophthalmia neonatorum and must be treated as urgent.

questions.q: Why does the module call fluorescein staining the pivotal step in a contact-lens wearer with a red eye?
ch: It measures the intraocular pressure without any instrument contacting the cornea
It confirms the presence of tender preauricular lymphadenopathy on the affected side
It identifies cobblestone papillae hidden on the everted upper eyelid
It distinguishes viral from bacterial discharge by staining the pus directly
It excludes corneal ulcer, abrasion, and a herpetic dendrite before any steroid is considered
questions.exp: Fluorescein with a cobalt-blue slit-lamp is mandatory in lens wearers or with pain or photophobia because it rules out corneal ulcer, abrasion, and a herpetic dendrite — and a dendrite absolutely forbids topical steroids.
why: Intraocular pressure is measured by tonometry, which belongs to the angle-closure workup.
Preauricular nodes are found by palpation, not by staining the surface of the cornea.
Papillae are seen by everting the lid, which is a separate part of the eye examination.
Fluorescein highlights corneal epithelial defects; it does not differentiate discharge types.

questions.q: A contact-lens wearer has purulent bacterial conjunctivitis. Which topical agent does the module prefer, and why?
ch: An aminoglycoside for prolonged use, because it penetrates lenses well
A fluoroquinolone, because it covers Pseudomonas in contact-lens wearers
Artificial tears alone, because all bacterial cases resolve on their own
Erythromycin ointment, because it is the best tolerated agent overnight
A topical corticosteroid, because it settles the inflammation fastest
questions.exp: Fluoroquinolone drops are preferred in contact-lens wearers specifically to cover Pseudomonas, the organism behind lens-related corneal ulcer.
why: Long-term aminoglycoside use is to be avoided because of corneal toxicity.
Many mild cases self-resolve, but a lens wearer is the exception in whom antibiotics are indicated.
Erythromycin ointment is an option in general bacterial disease but lacks Pseudomonas coverage.
Steroids must not be started empirically — they devastate a missed herpes keratitis and raise pressure.

questions.q: A young adult develops copious purulent discharge in one eye over 18 hours. What does the module direct you to do?
ch: Prescribe olopatadine drops and cold compresses for presumed allergy
Reassure and observe, since most conjunctivitis is self-limited over one to two weeks
Give IM ceftriaxone plus topical therapy, co-treat for chlamydia, and refer to ophthalmology urgently
Start a topical corticosteroid to prevent membrane formation on the lids
Send a viral panel and withhold all antibiotics pending the result
questions.exp: Hyperacute copious purulent discharge is gonococcal until proven otherwise and can perforate the cornea within days, so systemic ceftriaxone with topical therapy, chlamydia co-treatment, and urgent referral are required.
why: Antihistamine drops treat itching in allergic disease; this hyperacute purulent picture is an emergency.
Watchful waiting suits viral disease, not a cornea at risk of perforation within days.
Empiric steroids are contraindicated and would not address the underlying infection at all.
Cultures and Gram stain are indicated here, but treatment is presumptive and must not wait.

questions.q: Which infection-control instruction does the module give for active viral or bacterial conjunctivitis?
ch: Continue wearing contact lenses so they shield the cornea from irritants
Wipe the discharge from the outer canthus inward toward the nose
Keep the eye makeup and start reusing it once the discharge has cleared
Separate towels, no eye rubbing, discard eye makeup, and stay home while discharge is active
Share the same warm compress between both eyes to keep the eyelids soft
questions.exp: Hand hygiene plus separate towels, no eye rubbing, discarding eye makeup, and staying home from school or work while discharge is active are the module's infection-control measures.
why: Lens wear must stop until fully healed, and old lenses and the case are discarded.
The module directs wiping from the inner to the outer canthus, not the reverse direction.
Eye makeup is discarded rather than kept and reused after the discharge clears.
Sharing anything between the eyes spreads infection; gauze and supplies are used per eye.

questions.q: Which finding tells you a red eye is NOT simple conjunctivitis and needs escalation?
ch: Bilateral itching with stringy discharge and lid papillae
Eyelids stuck shut on waking with thick purulent discharge
Diffuse conjunctival redness with a normal visual acuity
Decreased visual acuity with severe eye pain and photophobia
Watery discharge with a tender preauricular lymph node
questions.exp: Reduced acuity, severe eye pain, or photophobia suggest keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than conjunctivitis, and are red flags to escalate.
why: Bilateral itching with papillae is allergic conjunctivitis and is managed medically.
Purulent discharge sticking the lids is ordinary bacterial conjunctivitis unless hyperacute.
Diffuse redness with normal acuity is the expected uncomplicated conjunctivitis pattern.
Watery discharge with a preauricular node is typical viral conjunctivitis, managed supportively.

questions.q: In uncomplicated conjunctivitis, what should the visual acuity and cornea look like?
ch: Acuity normal, with the sclera and cornea both remaining clear
Acuity reduced by two lines, with a hazy steamy cornea
Acuity normal, with a dendritic corneal lesion on staining
Acuity reduced, with a gray-green subretinal membrane
Acuity normal, with a fixed mid-dilated non-reactive pupil
questions.exp: Conjunctivitis dilates conjunctival vessels and produces discharge and irritation while visual acuity stays normal and the sclera and cornea remain clear.
why: A hazy steamy cornea with reduced acuity indicates acute angle-closure glaucoma.
A dendrite means herpes simplex keratitis and an absolute contraindication to topical steroids.
A subretinal membrane is a wet macular degeneration finding, unrelated to the conjunctiva.
A fixed mid-dilated pupil belongs to acute angle-closure glaucoma, not to conjunctivitis.

questions.q: A 4-day-old neonate has purulent conjunctival discharge. How does the module classify this?
ch: Urgent — treat any neonatal conjunctivitis as urgent and report it to the provider immediately
Self-limited viral disease requiring only hand hygiene and cool compresses
Routine bacterial conjunctivitis to treat with erythromycin ointment at home
Allergic conjunctivitis, since neonates are commonly atopic at this age
Chemical irritation that will resolve without any further evaluation
questions.exp: Neonatal conjunctivitis may be gonococcal, chlamydial, or chemical; the module says to treat any neonatal case as urgent, confirm erythromycin prophylaxis was given at birth, and notify the provider at once.
why: Self-limited viral disease is the adult pattern; a neonate is explicitly an exception.
Home treatment is unsafe here; a neonate needs urgent evaluation with cultures and NAAT testing.
Allergic disease presents with bilateral itching and papillae, not in a 4-day-old neonate.
Chemical irritation is one possible cause, but it cannot be assumed without evaluation.

questions.q: Which symptom triad does the module give for retinal detachment?
ch: Thick purulent discharge, lids stuck shut on waking, and normal acuity
Severe eye pain, halos around lights, and intractable vomiting
Intense itching, stringy mucoid discharge, and bilateral redness
Gradual central blur, wavy lines, and a need for brighter reading light
New flashes of light, a shower of new floaters, and a curtain over the peripheral field
questions.exp: The classic triad is new photopsia (flashes), a sudden increase in floaters, and a peripheral field defect described as a curtain, shadow, or veil — painless and progressive.
why: Purulent discharge with lids stuck shut and normal acuity is bacterial conjunctivitis.
Pain, halos, and vomiting form the acute angle-closure glaucoma triad instead.
Itching with stringy discharge and bilateral redness describes allergic conjunctivitis.
Central blur with wavy lines and needing brighter light is age-related macular degeneration.

questions.q: Which mechanism defines a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
ch: The peripheral iris occludes the trabecular meshwork and the pressure rises
Drusen accumulate under the retina and the pigment epithelium atrophies
A retinal tear or break lets liquefied vitreous seep under the retina
Fibrovascular bands pull the retina, as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Fluid leaks beneath the retina without any break, as with tumors or inflammation
questions.exp: Rhegmatogenous detachment — the most common type — occurs when a retinal tear or break allows liquefied vitreous to track into the subretinal space.
why: Iris occlusion of the meshwork is the mechanism of acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Drusen with pigment epithelial atrophy is dry age-related macular degeneration.
Traction from fibrovascular bands defines the tractional type, classically in diabetic retinopathy.
Fluid exuding without a break defines the exudative or serous type of detachment.

questions.q: What does the module mean by the phrase "mac-on = go"?
ch: Only mac-off detachments require a dilated fundoscopic examination and an OCT
A macula-off detachment must be taken to the operating room within minutes of presentation
Macular status does not affect the surgical timing at all, only the choice of procedure
A mac-on rhegmatogenous detachment is a surgical emergency, repaired within about 24 hours to protect central vision
The macula must already be detached before surgical repair can be attempted safely
questions.exp: An attached macula is a same-day surgical emergency — repair within roughly 24 hours preserves central vision — whereas a mac-off detachment is more time-flexible and carries a worse prognosis.
why: OCT is what determines macular status, so it is needed regardless of the answer.
It is the mac-on detachment that is emergent; mac-off is comparatively time-flexible.
Macular status is precisely what drives surgical urgency in this module.
Detaching the macula is exactly what surgery is racing to prevent, not a prerequisite.

questions.q: A patient has an intraocular SF6 gas bubble after vitrectomy. Which two exposures are absolutely contraindicated until it resorbs?
ch: Scleral depression and B-scan ocular ultrasound
Nitrous oxide anesthesia and air travel or high altitude
Topical timolol drops and oral acetazolamide
Cycloplegic drops and topical corticosteroids
Anti-VEGF injections and laser photocoagulation
questions.exp: Nitrous oxide and air travel or high altitude are absolute contraindications with an intraocular gas bubble, because gas expansion can spike the intraocular pressure and cause blindness.
why: Scleral depression and B-scan are diagnostic maneuvers, not contraindicated exposures.
Timolol and acetazolamide are used to manage gas-related pressure elevation, not avoided.
Cycloplegics and steroid drops are standard postoperative medications after surgical repair.
Anti-VEGF and laser address underlying drivers and retinal breaks; neither expands the bubble.

questions.q: What does Shafer's sign indicate on examination?
ch: Yellow lipid deposits accumulating beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
A corrugated, mobile retina visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy
Distortion of straight lines reported by the patient on an Amsler grid
A relative afferent pupillary defect caused by a large detachment
Pigmented "tobacco dust" cells in the anterior vitreous, strongly suggesting a retinal break
questions.exp: Shafer's sign is tobacco-dust pigment in the anterior vitreous and is highly suggestive of an associated retinal break, raising the pre-test probability of a tear substantially.
why: Yellow lipid deposits under the retina are drusen, seen in macular degeneration.
A corrugated mobile retina is the detachment itself, seen on dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy.
Amsler grid distortion is metamorphopsia, the red flag for wet macular degeneration.
An afferent pupillary defect is a separate finding signalling a large detachment, not tobacco dust.

questions.q: Which preoperative nursing instruction does the module give for a patient awaiting detachment repair?
ch: Have the patient sit fully upright at all times to drain subretinal fluid
Minimize head movement and avoid bending, straining, or heavy lifting
Encourage ambulation and light aerobic exercise to maintain circulation
Instill a mydriatic drop hourly to keep the pupil dilated overnight
Apply a firm pressure patch and irrigate the eyelids every hour
questions.exp: Activity restrictions before surgery — minimal head movement and no bending, straining, or heavy lifting — limit further detachment while the patient awaits repair.
why: Sitting fully upright is not prescribed; positioning matters after gas tamponade instead.
Ambulation and exercise increase head movement, which the module says to minimize.
Hourly dilation is not described; the drop teaching concerns postoperative medications.
Pressure patching and lid irrigation are not part of the described preoperative care.

questions.q: The module matches the repair procedure to the anatomy. Which pairing does it give?
ch: Pneumatic retinopexy is preferred for complex pseudophakic detachments with media opacity
Trabeculectomy is the operation of choice for a single superior retinal break
A scleral buckle is preferred when the vitreous cavity view is obscured by hemorrhage
Pneumatic retinopexy for a single superior break, scleral buckle in younger phakic patients, vitrectomy for complex cases
Laser peripheral iridotomy repairs tractional detachment in proliferative diabetic retinopathy
questions.exp: Pneumatic retinopexy suits a single superior break, a scleral buckle is favored in younger phakic patients, and vitrectomy is chosen for complex, pseudophakic, or media-opacifying cases.
why: Complex, pseudophakic, or media-opacifying cases go to vitrectomy, not pneumatic retinopexy.
Trabeculectomy is glaucoma surgery and has no role in repairing a retinal break.
An obscured view favors vitrectomy; the buckle is favored in younger phakic eyes.
Laser iridotomy relieves pupillary block in angle closure, not tractional detachment.

questions.q: A high myope reports new floaters and a temporal shadow three months after cataract surgery. Why do these two facts matter mechanistically?
ch: Axial elongation thins the peripheral retina and cataract surgery accelerates vitreous liquefaction
Both of them produce drusen and geographic atrophy at the central macula
Both of them cause conjunctival inflammation that mimics a true field defect
Both of them raise intraocular pressure and close the anterior chamber angle
Both of them cause VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization beneath the macula
questions.exp: Axial elongation in high myopia thins the peripheral retina, and cataract surgery accelerates vitreous liquefaction and posterior vitreous detachment — the two mechanisms the module links to retinal breaks.
why: Drusen and geographic atrophy are macular degeneration findings, not detachment mechanisms.
Conjunctival inflammation does not produce a peripheral field defect of this kind.
Neither is described as raising pressure or closing the angle; that is angle-closure glaucoma.
Choroidal neovascularization is the wet macular degeneration mechanism, not a detachment one.

questions.q: A patient reports new flashes and floaters but has no field loss at all. What does the module say to do?
ch: Order a B-scan ultrasound only if the acuity drops below 20/40
Start topical timolol to lower the intraocular pressure prophylactically
Perform a dilated exam, since any acute PVD warrants exclusion of a retinal break
Reassure and follow up in one year, since a field defect is absent
Begin anti-VEGF injections to prevent progression to a detachment
questions.exp: Any acute posterior vitreous detachment warrants a dilated examination to exclude a break, and Shafer's sign or vitreous hemorrhage raises the pre-test probability of a tear substantially.
why: B-scan is used when the view is obscured, not gated on a visual acuity threshold.
Pressure-lowering drops address postoperative or gas-related elevation, not a PVD.
Flashes and floaters without field loss still require a dilated exam to exclude a break.
Anti-VEGF treats the drivers of tractional and exudative disease, not an acute PVD.

questions.q: Two days after vitrectomy with gas tamponade a patient reports severe eye pain, nausea, and halos. What does this suggest?
ch: Dangerous intraocular pressure elevation requiring urgent treatment
Endophthalmitis that mandates immediate intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
Recurrent macular detachment that will resolve with positioning alone
An allergic reaction to the cycloplegic drop, treated by stopping it
Normal postoperative discomfort that needs only oral analgesia
questions.exp: In a patient with an intraocular gas bubble, severe eye pain, nausea, or halos signals dangerous pressure elevation and is treated urgently with agents such as timolol or acetazolamide.
why: Infection is a concern after intraocular surgery, but anti-VEGF is not a treatment for it.
Recurrent detachment presents as a new curtain or worsening vision, not this pressure picture.
Cycloplegics cause blurred near vision and photophobia, not this pain-nausea-halo cluster.
The module lists this cluster as a red flag, not as expected postoperative discomfort.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes dry from wet age-related macular degeneration?
ch: Dry = closed anterior chamber angle; wet = open angle with elevated pressure
Dry = drusen and RPE atrophy; wet = VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization
Dry = choroidal neovascularization; wet = drusen and pigment epithelial atrophy
Dry = peripheral field loss; wet = optic disc cupping and a high pressure
Dry = retinal tear with subretinal fluid; wet = fibrovascular vitreous traction
questions.exp: Dry (non-exudative) AMD is drusen accumulation with retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, while wet (exudative) AMD is VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization with leakage and hemorrhage.
why: Angle status describes glaucoma; the anterior chamber is not involved in AMD.
This reverses the two: neovascularization defines the wet form and drusen the dry form.
Peripheral field loss and disc cupping describe glaucoma, not macular degeneration.
Retinal tears and vitreous traction are retinal detachment mechanisms instead.

questions.q: How does the module describe the relative frequency and impact of wet AMD?
ch: About half of all cases, and it carries the mildest visual consequences
About 85-90% of cases, progressing slowly toward geographic atrophy
About 10-15% of cases, but responsible for most severe vision loss
About 10-15% of cases, and it never threatens the central acuity
About 30% of cases, and it is prevented entirely by AREDS2 supplements
questions.exp: Wet (exudative) AMD accounts for roughly 10-15% of cases yet causes most of the severe vision loss, because leaky choroidal vessels produce rapid fluid, hemorrhage, and scarring.
why: Wet AMD is the minority of cases and has the most severe consequences, not the mildest.
The figure of 85-90% with slow progression to geographic atrophy describes the dry form.
The frequency is right, but wet AMD is precisely what destroys central acuity rapidly.
AREDS2 slows progression in intermediate or advanced dry disease; it does not prevent AMD.

questions.q: What functional pattern of vision loss does the module attribute to AMD?
ch: Complete blindness in most patients within a year of the diagnosis
Loss of peripheral vision with fully preserved reading ability
Painful loss of vision that begins with halos around lights
Tunnel vision progressing down to a small central island
Loss of reading, driving, and face recognition, with peripheral vision spared
questions.exp: AMD attacks the central retina, so patients lose the ability to read, drive, and recognize faces while peripheral vision is spared — they rarely go completely blind.
why: Peripheral vision is spared, so these patients rarely go completely blind.
This is reversed: central vision is lost and reading is what fails first.
Painful loss with halos around lights describes acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Tunnel vision narrowing to a central island is the glaucomatous field sequence.

questions.q: A patient with intermediate dry AMD reports that straight lines suddenly look wavy. What does this most likely represent?
ch: A retinal detachment, since flashes and floaters always precede distortion
A side effect of the AREDS2 supplement that resolves once it is stopped
Expected progression of drusen that warrants only routine yearly follow-up
Metamorphopsia signalling conversion to wet AMD — an urgent referral
A cataract requiring surgical extraction before the vision can improve
questions.exp: New metamorphopsia — wavy lines on the Amsler grid — is the classic red flag for conversion to wet AMD and prompts urgent referral for possible same-day anti-VEGF treatment.
why: Detachment presents with flashes, floaters, and a peripheral curtain, not central distortion.
No such supplement effect is described; AREDS2 slows progression and does not distort vision.
Sudden distortion is not routine drusen progression; it demands urgent rather than yearly review.
Cataract causes gradual blur and glare, not new central distortion of straight lines.

questions.q: For which patient does the module say AREDS2 supplementation is indicated?
ch: A patient with no drusen at all but a strong family history of AMD
Any adult over 50 as primary prevention against developing AMD
A patient with early AMD and small drusen only on fundoscopy
A patient with wet AMD, used in place of anti-VEGF injections
A patient with intermediate AMD, or with advanced disease in one eye
questions.exp: AREDS2 slows progression in intermediate or advanced (one-eye) dry AMD; it does not prevent early AMD and does not restore vision that has already been lost.
why: Family history raises risk but is not itself an indication for supplementation.
Supplements do not prevent AMD, so blanket use as primary prevention is not supported.
Early AMD with small drusen falls explicitly outside the benefit shown for AREDS2.
Wet AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF; supplements do not replace those injections.

questions.q: Why did AREDS2 replace beta-carotene with lutein and zeaxanthin?
ch: Beta-carotene raised the intraocular pressure in treated patients
Beta-carotene caused zinc-induced copper deficiency anemia in treated patients
Beta-carotene was found to accelerate choroidal neovascularization
Beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers
Lutein and zeaxanthin restore vision that has already been lost
questions.exp: Beta-carotene was dropped because it increased lung cancer risk in smokers and lutein with zeaxanthin was substituted; copper is added separately to prevent zinc-induced copper deficiency anemia.
why: Raised intraocular pressure is a steroid and injection concern, not a supplement effect.
Copper is added to the formula to prevent zinc-induced copper deficiency — a different issue.
No acceleration of neovascularization by beta-carotene is described in the module.
Neither carotenoid restores lost vision; the supplement only slows progression.

questions.q: What role does the module assign to OCT in age-related macular degeneration?
ch: A screening test that replaces dilated fundoscopic examination entirely
Key confirmatory imaging showing intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and it guides anti-VEGF re-treatment
A dye-based angiographic test that localizes choroidal neovascular leakage
A home self-monitoring tool that the patient uses once daily in each eye
The reference standard for measuring the intraocular pressure accurately
questions.exp: OCT is the key confirmatory imaging — a non-invasive cross-section showing intraretinal and subretinal fluid plus drusen — and it guides diagnosis and anti-VEGF re-treatment decisions.
why: Dilated fundoscopy remains the core exam; OCT confirms rather than replaces it.
Fluorescein angiography is the dye-based study that localizes CNV leakage; OCT uses no dye.
The Amsler grid is the home self-monitoring tool; OCT is performed in the office.
Pressure is measured by tonometry, which belongs to the glaucoma workup instead.

questions.q: A patient reports eye pain, increasing redness, discharge, and worsening vision three days after an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. What must be excluded?
ch: A systemic thromboembolic event caused by the injected drug
Failure of the AREDS2 supplement to slow the progression
Endophthalmitis, a sight-threatening emergency
Expected mild irritation and floaters following the injection
Progression of geographic atrophy within the treated eye
questions.exp: Pain, increasing redness, discharge, photophobia, or worsening vision after an intravitreal injection suggest endophthalmitis — a sight-threatening emergency to report and evaluate urgently.
why: Thromboembolic events are a rare systemic risk and would not present as a painful red eye.
Supplement failure is not an acute event and is unrelated to the injection itself.
Mild irritation and floaters can be normal, but pain with redness, discharge, and vision loss are not.
Geographic atrophy enlarges slowly over months and does not cause acute pain and discharge.

questions.q: Which intervention does the module call the single most important modifiable step to reduce AMD progression?
ch: Smoking cessation, alongside cardiovascular risk factor control
Beginning prophylactic anti-VEGF injections before any CNV appears
Referral for low-vision rehabilitation with magnifiers and lighting
Daily Amsler grid self-monitoring performed at home in each eye
Starting AREDS2 supplements in every patient over the age of 50
questions.exp: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor, so cessation — with blood-pressure control, a leafy-green and fish-rich diet, and UV protection — is the single most important intervention.
why: Anti-VEGF is treatment for established neovascularization, not a prophylactic measure.
Low-vision rehabilitation preserves function but does not slow the disease progression.
The Amsler grid detects conversion early; it does not itself reduce progression.
Supplements are for intermediate or advanced disease and are not the top modifiable factor.

questions.q: What does the module say about pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol in advanced dry AMD?
ch: They slow geographic atrophy growth without improving vision, and can convert dry AMD to wet
They eliminate the need for any continued smoking cessation counseling
They reverse geographic atrophy and restore the lost central visual acuity
They are oral agents taken alongside the AREDS2 supplement formulation
They are first-line therapy for wet AMD, replacing anti-VEGF injections
questions.exp: These intravitreal complement inhibitors slow the enlargement of geographic atrophy but do not improve vision, and they carry a risk of converting dry AMD to neovascular disease and of intraocular inflammation.
why: Smoking cessation remains the top modifiable intervention regardless of any therapy.
They slow lesion enlargement; they neither reverse atrophy nor restore acuity.
They are intravitreal agents given in the office, not oral supplements.
Anti-VEGF agents remain first-line for wet AMD; complement inhibitors target dry disease.
